plan.title: Kindle vs Paper Books: Which Helps You Remember?
plan.description: A quick comparison of reading on a Kindle and in print, based on research into comprehension and memory. Learn where paper has an edge and when a Kindle is fine.

beats.narration: You finish a novel on your Kindle. Then someone asks what happened first. You freeze. Research suggests that is not just you. The screen may change what you remember.

clip_queries: hands turning pages of a book
props.alt: woman using tablet reader at home

beats.narration: A 2018 meta-analysis pulled together 54 experiments. Its verdict was clear: paper has an advantage for comprehension. Other studies found no difference, so the debate is real, but the larger evidence leans toward print.

props.label: experiments reviewed in a 2018 meta-analysis: paper came out ahead

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: In one study of a long story, readers scored the same on most tests. But on chronology, the order of events, paper readers did better than Kindle readers.

props.verdict: Paper helps you remember when things happened

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Why? A page gives physical cues: where you are, how thick the pile is behind you. A screen gives fewer. Readers may build a weaker mental map of the story.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Does that mean ditch your Kindle? No. For light reading, or when you travel, it is fine. For a story you want to remember, or something to study, choose paper.

accuracy.reason: The 54-experiment 2018 meta-analysis and the chronology finding match the notes. But "the larger evidence leans toward print" and "the medium shapes memory" overstate correlational findings. The "how thick the pile is behind you" detail is unsourced and the notes frame the effect as comprehension, not memory.

coverage.reason: The brief asked for portability, eye strain, battery, feel, price and environment. The script covers only comprehension and a passing mention of travel. Eye strain, battery, price and environmental impact are all missing.

structure.reason: Clean arc from hook to evidence to mechanism to advice to takeaway, with no repetition and good pacing for one minute.

hook_ending.reason: The opening scenario of freezing when asked what happened first is a relatable hook. The closing line "when it matters, hold the book" is memorable, though it is slightly preachy.

tone.reason: Conversational and clear for a general US audience, and it hedges with "may" and "suggests".

visuals.reason: Scene types vary: stat, versus, diagram, checklist and kinetic text. The stat "54" is a genuine number. The versus table is slightly redundant with the narration.

originality.reason: The chronology finding is a specific, less obvious fact. The framing is otherwise generic and drawn from a single research angle.

instructions.reason: The script is a one-sided memory comparison, not the fair, multi-factor comparison requested. The takeaway by reader type is thin and the script leans toward paper. Length is about right.

language.reason: Fluent, natural and grammatical, with short punchy sentences.

defects.quote: For light reading, or when you travel, it is fine.
defects.issue: Omits eye strain, battery life, price, the feel of the book and the environmental angle. Portability gets only a passing mention.
The title and framing narrow a requested fair general comparison to a single memory question, so the video is biased toward paper.

defects.quote: Its verdict was clear: paper has an advantage for comprehension.
defects.issue: The meta-analysis was mostly about screens in general, not Kindles, and the effect is stronger for informational texts and under time pressure. Presenting it as a Kindle-vs-book verdict overgeneralizes.

defects.quote: how thick the pile is behind you
defects.issue: This specific detail is not in the notes, and the single small study is stretched into an advice rule.
This is a causal claim, stated more strongly than the hedged evidence supports.

missing: Eye strain, e-ink versus backlit screens

wrong_facts: Overstated: "the larger evidence leans toward print" and "the medium shapes memory" go beyond the hedged findings, and the 'pile of pages' cue detail is unsourced.
judge.summary: A well-written, tightly structured script with a good hook, but it narrows the topic to reading comprehension and skips most of the requested comparison points (eye strain, battery, price, environment). The overall tilt toward paper makes it less fair than the brief asked for.
